nodes.label: Scientific models and theories develop over time with new data
nodes.objective: Explain how new experimental data can lead to changes in scientific models or theories.
essentialPoints: Scientific theories are provisional and change when new evidence is found
New data can support, refine or overturn existing models
Deciding whether given data supports a theory is a testable skill

nodes.label: Using scientific models to explain, predict and show limitations
nodes.objective: Use representational, spatial, descriptive and mathematical models to explain phenomena, make predictions and recognise their limitations.
essentialPoints: Models (diagrams, equations, representations) simplify real phenomena
Models can be used to make predictions or calculate quantities
Models have limitations and can be tested against experimental observation

nodes.label: Power and limitations of science; ethical issues
nodes.objective: Explain why scientific data may be uncertain or incomplete, and outline ethical arguments about new technologies.
essentialPoints: Data is needed to answer scientific questions but may be incomplete or uncertain
Science cannot answer questions of ethics, only inform them
Ethical arguments weigh rights and wrongs of new technology

nodes.label: Evaluating applications and implications of science
nodes.objective: Describe and evaluate technological applications of science including personal, social, economic and environmental implications.
essentialPoints: Applications of science have personal, social, economic and environmental impacts
Decisions about science-based issues should be based on evaluation of evidence and arguments

nodes.label: Evaluating risk in practical science and society
nodes.objective: Evaluate risks in practical work and wider society, and explain why perceived risk differs from measured risk.
essentialPoints: Hazards of science-based technologies must be weighed against benefits
Perceived risk can differ from actual/measured risk (voluntary vs imposed, familiar vs unfamiliar, visible vs invisible)

nodes.label: Peer review and communicating scientific results
nodes.objective: Explain the purpose of peer review and why media reports of science may be unreliable.
essentialPoints: Peer review checks scientific claims before publication to detect false claims and build consensus
Media reports are not peer reviewed and may be oversimplified, inaccurate or biased

nodes.label: Forming a hypothesis from scientific theory
nodes.objective: Suggest a testable hypothesis to explain given observations or data using scientific theory.
essentialPoints: A hypothesis is a testable explanation based on existing scientific theory
Hypotheses are proposed to explain observations before testing

nodes.label: Independent, dependent and control variables
nodes.objective: Identify and explain the role of independent, dependent and control variables in an investigation.
essentialPoints: The independent variable is the one changed or selected by the investigator
The dependent variable is measured for each change in the independent variable
Control variables are kept constant to ensure a fair test

nodes.label: Planning experimental procedures
nodes.objective: Plan or devise an experimental procedure to test a hypothesis, make observations, or characterise a substance, controlling relevant variables.
essentialPoints: A well-designed procedure controls variables to allow valid conclusions
Procedures must be suited to their specific purpose (observation, testing, characterisation)

nodes.label: Selecting appropriate apparatus, techniques and materials
nodes.objective: Select and justify the technique, instrument, apparatus or material appropriate for a given experimental purpose.
essentialPoints: Different instruments/apparatus suit different purposes and required precision
Justification of choice depends on the specific experimental context

nodes.label: Identifying hazards and reducing risk in practical work
nodes.objective: Identify hazards in practical contexts and suggest methods to reduce the risk of harm.
essentialPoints: Hazards must be identified before carrying out practical work
Risk of harm can be reduced through specific precautions relevant to the hazard

nodes.label: Sampling techniques to obtain representative samples
nodes.objective: Suggest and describe an appropriate sampling technique to ensure samples collected are representative.
essentialPoints: A representative sample reflects the properties of the whole population or material being tested
Sampling technique choice depends on the context and material

nodes.label: Making and recording measurements using apparatus
nodes.objective: Make and record observations and measurements accurately using a range of apparatus, reading scales correctly.
essentialPoints: Measurements must be read correctly off analogue and digital scales
Measurements should be recorded with appropriate precision and units

nodes.label: Evaluating methods and validity
nodes.objective: Evaluate whether an experimental method is valid and whether sufficient, precise measurements were taken, suggesting improvements.
essentialPoints: Validity means the method actually tests what it claims to test, with controlled variables
Sufficiency and precision of measurements should be assessed
Improvements can be suggested to address weaknesses in a method

nodes.label: Constructing and interpreting frequency tables, bar charts and histograms
nodes.objective: Construct and interpret frequency tables, bar charts and histograms from data.
essentialPoints: Frequency tables organise raw data into categories or intervals
Bar charts and histograms are used to display and interpret this data visually

nodes.label: Plotting two variables from experimental data
nodes.objective: Plot two variables from experimental or other data onto a graph with appropriate axes and scales.
essentialPoints: Independent variable is plotted on the x-axis, dependent on the y-axis
Axes must be scaled and labelled appropriately with units

nodes.label: Translating data between graphical and numeric forms
nodes.objective: Convert data between tabular/numeric form and graphical representation.
essentialPoints: Data presented as a table can be represented as a graph and vice versa
Choosing the correct representation depends on the type of data (continuous/discrete)

nodes.label: Using appropriate significant figures
nodes.objective: Use an appropriate number of significant figures when reporting calculated or measured values.
essentialPoints: The number of significant figures in an answer should reflect the precision of the data given
Rounding rules apply consistently when stating final answers

nodes.label: Calculating arithmetic mean and range
nodes.objective: Calculate the arithmetic mean and range of a set of repeated measurements.
essentialPoints: The mean is the sum of values divided by the number of values
The range is the difference between the highest and lowest value in a data set

nodes.label: Making order of magnitude calculations
nodes.objective: Make estimates of quantities to the correct order of magnitude, using powers of ten.
essentialPoints: An order of magnitude estimate expresses a quantity as a power of ten
Used to sanity-check whether a calculated answer is reasonable

nodes.label: Changing the subject of an equation
nodes.objective: Rearrange an algebraic equation to make a different quantity the subject.
essentialPoints: Rearranging isolates the required unknown quantity on one side of the equation
The same operation must be applied to both sides to preserve equality

nodes.label: Substituting values into equations with correct units
nodes.objective: Substitute numerical values into algebraic equations using appropriate units for physical quantities.
essentialPoints: Every value substituted must be expressed in consistent units before calculation
The final answer must include the correct unit

nodes.label: Determining slope and intercept of a linear graph
nodes.objective: Determine the gradient and y-intercept of a straight-line graph and relate this to y = mx + c.
essentialPoints: The gradient is calculated as change in y divided by change in x
The y-intercept is the value of y where the line crosses the y-axis
A straight-line graph follows the form y = mx + c

nodes.label: Using the tangent to a curve to find rate of change
nodes.objective: Draw a tangent to a point on a curve and use its slope as a measure of the instantaneous rate of change.
essentialPoints: A tangent is a straight line touching a curve at a single point
The gradient of the tangent gives the instantaneous rate of change at that point

nodes.label: Finding area between a curve and the x-axis
nodes.objective: Understand the physical significance of the area between a curve and the x-axis and measure it by counting squares.
essentialPoints: The area under a graph can represent a physically meaningful quantity
This area can be estimated by counting the squares beneath the curve

nodes.label: Estimating uncertainty using the range about the mean
nodes.objective: Recognise that all measurements have uncertainty and use the range of repeat measurements about the mean as an estimate of this uncertainty.
essentialPoints: Every measurement carries some degree of uncertainty
The range of repeated measurements about the mean can be used to estimate uncertainty

nodes.label: Interpreting data: patterns, trends, inferences and conclusions
nodes.objective: Interpret data presented in verbal, diagrammatic, graphical, symbolic or numerical form to identify patterns, make inferences and draw conclusions.
essentialPoints: Patterns and trends in data can be identified across different presentation formats
Conclusions must be drawn directly from, and supported by, the data given
Data can be used to make predictions

nodes.label: Relating data to hypotheses and reasoned explanations
nodes.objective: Present reasoned explanations relating experimental data to a hypothesis, including comparing competing hypotheses.
essentialPoints: The extent to which data supports or contradicts a hypothesis can be commented on
Where multiple hypotheses exist, data can be used to judge which is better supported

nodes.label: Accuracy, precision, repeatability and reproducibility
nodes.objective: Distinguish between accuracy, precision, repeatability and reproducibility when evaluating data.
essentialPoints: An accurate measurement is close to the true value
Precise measurements cluster closely together
Repeatable results are obtained by the same investigator using the same method and equipment
Reproducible results are obtained by different investigators or different equipment

nodes.label: Random error, systematic error and anomalous results
nodes.objective: Identify potential sources of random and systematic error, and explain how to treat anomalous values.
essentialPoints: Random error causes results to vary unpredictably and can be reduced by taking more measurements and finding a mean
Systematic error causes results to differ from the true value by a consistent amount each time
Anomalous values should be investigated and, if due to poor measurement, discarded

nodes.label: Evaluating data quality to suggest improvements
nodes.objective: Use accuracy, precision, repeatability, reproducibility and error types to evaluate data and suggest improvements to procedures.
essentialPoints: Evaluating data quality requires combining knowledge of accuracy, precision, repeatability, reproducibility and error type
Suggested improvements should target the specific identified source of error or imprecision

nodes.label: Communicating scientific rationale, methods, findings and conclusions
nodes.objective: Present coherent, logically structured reports of investigations covering rationale, method, findings and conclusions.
essentialPoints: A scientific report should logically link rationale, method, findings and conclusion
Findings should be communicated using verbal, diagrammatic, graphical, numerical or symbolic forms as appropriate

nodes.label: Using scientific vocabulary, terminology and definitions
nodes.objective: Use correct scientific vocabulary, terminology and definitions when communicating chemistry.
essentialPoints: Correct scientific terms must be used precisely rather than everyday synonyms
Definitions of key terms must be stated accurately

nodes.label: Scientific quantities and how they are determined
nodes.objective: Recognise the importance of scientific quantities and understand how they are determined experimentally.
essentialPoints: A scientific quantity has both a numerical value and a unit
Quantities are determined through defined measurement procedures

nodes.label: Using SI units and chemical nomenclature
nodes.objective: Use SI units (e.g. kg, g, mg, km, m, mm, kJ, J) and IUPAC chemical nomenclature correctly.
essentialPoints: SI units are the standard units used to express physical quantities in science
IUPAC nomenclature provides standardised chemical naming

nodes.label: Using prefixes and powers of ten for orders of magnitude
nodes.objective: Use standard prefixes (tera, giga, mega, kilo, centi, milli, micro, nano) and powers of ten to express orders of magnitude.
essentialPoints: Prefixes represent specific powers of ten applied to a base unit
Powers of ten allow very large or very small quantities to be expressed concisely

nodes.label: Interconverting units
nodes.objective: Convert measurements between related units, including using prefixes and standard form.
essentialPoints: Converting units requires knowing the relationship (conversion factor) between them
Prefixes and powers of ten are used to convert between multiples of a base unit

nodes.label: Recognising and using standard form
nodes.objective: Recognise and use numbers expressed in standard form (A × 10^n).
essentialPoints: Standard form expresses numbers as a value between 1 and 10 multiplied by a power of ten
Standard form is used for very large or very small numbers

nodes.label: Recognising and using decimal form
nodes.objective: Recognise and use expressions in decimal form in calculations and measurements.
essentialPoints: Decimal numbers represent quantities that are not whole numbers
Decimal place value determines precision of a measurement or calculation

nodes.label: Using ratios, fractions and percentages
nodes.objective: Use ratios, fractions and percentages to solve numerical problems in chemistry contexts.
essentialPoints: Ratios compare quantities relative to each other
Fractions and percentages express a part relative to a whole

nodes.label: Estimating the results of calculations
nodes.objective: Make estimates of the results of simple calculations to check plausibility of an answer.
essentialPoints: An estimate uses rounded values to quickly approximate a calculation result
Estimation is used to check whether a calculated answer is reasonable

nodes.label: Understanding and using algebraic/mathematical symbols
nodes.objective: Understand and use the symbols =, <, <<, >>, >, ∝ and ~ correctly in scientific contexts.
essentialPoints: Each symbol has a precise mathematical meaning (equals, less than, much less than, much greater than, greater than, proportional to, approximately equal to)
Correct use of these symbols is required when expressing relationships between quantities

nodes.label: Understanding y = mx + c as a linear relationship
nodes.objective: Understand that y = mx + c represents a linear relationship between two variables.
essentialPoints: m represents the gradient of the line and c represents the y-intercept
A linear relationship produces a straight-line graph

nodes.label: Visualising and representing 2D and 3D forms
nodes.objective: Visualise and represent 2D and 3D forms, including 2D representations of 3D objects such as molecular structures.
essentialPoints: 3D structures (e.g. molecules, crystal lattices) can be represented in 2D diagrams
Interpreting 2D representations requires visualising the true 3D shape

nodes.label: Calculating areas and volumes of simple shapes
nodes.objective: Calculate areas of triangles and rectangles, and surface areas and volumes of cubes.
essentialPoints: Area of a rectangle = length × width; area of a triangle = 0.5 × base × height
Volume of a cube = side length cubed; surface area = 6 × side length squared

nodes.label: Reading measurement scales (volume, mass, temperature)
nodes.objective: Read analogue and digital scales correctly, including measuring cylinders, balances, thermometers and burettes, to the appropriate precision.
essentialPoints: The scale must be read at eye level, taking the meniscus into account for liquids
Readings should be recorded to the precision of the smallest graduation on the instrument

nodes.label: Using a top-pan balance to measure mass
nodes.objective: Correctly zero (tare) and use a top-pan balance to measure the mass of a substance or container.
essentialPoints: A balance must be tared/zeroed with any container before adding the substance
Readings should be recorded to the precision shown on the balance display

nodes.label: Safe use of heating apparatus (Bunsen burner, water bath)
nodes.objective: Set up and safely use a Bunsen burner or water bath to heat substances in practical investigations.
essentialPoints: A Bunsen burner should be used with a yellow (safety) flame when not actively heating and blue flame when heating
A water bath provides gentler, more even heating than a direct flame for temperature-sensitive substances

nodes.label: Carrying out filtration to separate an insoluble solid from a liquid
nodes.objective: Set up filter paper and funnel correctly to separate an insoluble solid (residue) from a liquid (filtrate).
essentialPoints: Filter paper is folded and placed in a funnel to trap insoluble solid while liquid passes through
The residue remains on the filter paper and the filtrate is collected below

nodes.label: Carrying out an acid-base titration using a burette
nodes.objective: Use a burette, pipette and indicator to accurately measure the volume of solution needed to reach an end point in a titration.
essentialPoints: A pipette delivers a fixed, accurate volume of one solution into a conical flask
A burette is used to add the second solution gradually, reading the volume at the meniscus to the nearest graduation
An indicator is used to identify the end point of the reaction
Repeat titrations should be carried out until concordant results (within 0.10 cm3) are obtained

nodes.label: Collecting and measuring gas volume produced in a reaction
nodes.objective: Set up apparatus (e.g. gas syringe or inverted measuring cylinder over water) to collect and measure the volume of gas produced over time.
essentialPoints: A gas syringe measures the volume of gas produced directly and accurately
Collection over water can be used for gases that are insoluble in water
Volume readings are taken at fixed time intervals to monitor reaction progress

nodes.label: Taking timed readings at fixed intervals
nodes.objective: Take measurements at regular, fixed time intervals during a reaction to monitor how a variable changes over time.
essentialPoints: Consistent, regular time intervals allow rate of change to be tracked and compared fairly
A stopwatch or timer is started at a defined starting point (e.g. mixing of reagents)

nodes.label: Monitoring temperature change during a reaction
nodes.objective: Use a thermometer or temperature probe correctly to monitor and record temperature changes during a chemical reaction.
essentialPoints: The thermometer bulb/probe should be immersed fully in the reacting mixture without touching the container
The maximum or minimum temperature change is recorded relative to the starting temperature

nodes.label: Preparing solutions of known concentration
nodes.objective: Accurately prepare a solution of known concentration by dissolving a known mass of solute in a known volume of solvent, or by dilution.
essentialPoints: A known mass of solute is dissolved and made up to a precise volume using a volumetric flask
Dilution reduces concentration by a calculable factor when a stock solution is diluted with a known volume of solvent

nodes.label: Carrying out paper chromatography
nodes.objective: Set up and run a paper chromatography experiment, applying samples correctly and calculating Rf values from the result.
essentialPoints: A pencil baseline is used to spot samples above the level of the solvent
The solvent front and spot positions are measured to calculate Rf values

nodes.label: Setting up electrolysis apparatus
nodes.objective: Correctly set up electrodes, electrolyte and power supply to carry out electrolysis safely and observe products at each electrode.
essentialPoints: Electrodes must be connected to the correct terminals of the power supply and immersed in the electrolyte without touching
Products at each electrode are identified and observed separately

nodes.label: Measuring pH using indicators or a probe
nodes.objective: Use universal indicator/pH paper or a pH probe correctly to measure and record the pH of a solution.
essentialPoints: Universal indicator or pH paper is compared to a colour chart to estimate pH
A calibrated pH probe gives a more precise numerical pH reading
